Build a retirement-income bridge: map the years before later income begins

Four graphics connect income start dates, temporary work, annual withdrawal requests and the capital needed over a defined retirement transition.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a retirement-income bridge

Interactive planning lab

Starting capital for all modeled withdrawals$264,151.23
Cumulative unfunded withdrawals$95,914.67

Hypothetical annual net cash flows over the selected horizon, not a lifetime retirement projection. Spending and all income inputs are stated in year-1 CAD and increase at the same selected rate. Temporary work ends after the selected years; additional income begins in the selected start year. Income arrives and withdrawals occur at year-end, after the portfolio earns its constant effective annual return. Withdrawals are capped at available assets, with unmet amounts recorded separately. Surplus income is not added to the portfolio. No tax, benefit eligibility, pension quotations, start-age adjustments, mortality or stochastic returns are calculated. No spending or terminal capital requirement beyond the horizon is included.

The central idea

A retirement plan needs a calendar as well as a total. Temporary earnings may end before another income source starts, leaving a larger withdrawal request in the intervening years.

01

Draw the income calendar before choosing a withdrawal amount

Retirement rarely replaces one paycheque with a single identical payment. An ongoing pension, temporary work, a later pension and personal savings can each follow a different schedule. The Government of Canada’s retirement-income overview describes public pensions, workplace plans and personal savings as separate sources. Actual benefits depend on their own rules and the individual’s history.

This illustration starts with net amounts available to the household. It does not estimate pension entitlements or calculate tax. Enter a spending target, income already available, temporary work and an additional income source with its own starting year. All amounts use year-one purchasing power and then rise at the selected common annual rate.

The first chart compares the resulting annual spending and income paths. It makes changes in the funding mix visible before a portfolio withdrawal rule is applied. The additional-income amount stays the same in year-one dollars when its start date changes; no delayed-pension enhancement is assumed.

02

Notice the years between temporary work and later income

The default target is CAD 60,000 a year, with CAD 18,000 of ongoing income and CAD 12,000 of temporary work for three years. Year one therefore asks savings to supply CAD 30,000. With the selected 2% annual cash-flow increase, the next two requests are CAD 30,600 and CAD 31,212.

Temporary work then ends, while the additional income does not start until year six. The year-four withdrawal request rises to CAD 44,570.74 and year five to CAD 45,462.15. Those amounts reflect both the income interruption and the common annual increase. A flat average across the full horizon would hide the timing of the larger requests.

In year six, the additional CAD 24,000 of annual income, stated in year-one dollars, becomes available. The nominal gap falls to CAD 19,873.45. It does not disappear because the combined ongoing sources still cover only CAD 42,000 of the CAD 60,000 base spending target.

03

Separate the bridge subtotal from the full illustration

The first metric adds withdrawal requests in the years before the additional source begins. In the default case, that is approximately CAD 181,844.89 over the first five years. It is an undiscounted nominal subtotal, rather than the capital needed on the starting date.

The capital metric instead discounts every requested withdrawal across the selected twelve-year horizon. The formula is starting capital = sum of each year’s requested withdrawal divided by (1 + return) raised to that year. At the default constant 4% annual return, the result is approximately CAD 264,151.23.

This amount funds only the displayed withdrawals under the selected timing. It requires no terminal reserve and includes no expenses after year twelve. Calling it a complete retirement target would overlook the rest of the person’s life, as well as uncertain returns, taxes and changing needs.

04

Keep unfunded spending separate from portfolio assets

The portfolio chart starts with CAD 200,000 in the default example. Each year, the balance earns the assumed return before the requested year-end withdrawal. The actual withdrawal cannot exceed available assets. Any difference is added to a separate cumulative unfunded-spending series.

After depletion, the portfolio remains at zero; this model adds no new deposits. The unfunded curve is neither an investment account nor an available credit line. It records spending the assumed portfolio could not supply, without assuming that spending was financed elsewhere.

If income exceeds spending, the withdrawal request is zero. That surplus is left unallocated rather than automatically saved. A real plan can assign it a destination, but doing so would introduce an additional decision about contributions, access and future use.

05

Test the bridge without turning it into a pension recommendation

The matrix changes the spending target and the later-income start year, keeping the selected return, horizon, temporary-work schedule and income amount. Its cells use the full-horizon present-value calculation. Changing a date can alter capital needs even when the annual income amount is unchanged.

Actual CPP, OAS or workplace-pension timing may also change benefit amounts, tax, eligibility and household outcomes. Those effects are outside this generic calendar. Use current personal estimates and the relevant program rules before comparing an actual start-age choice.

Review the bridge alongside the sequence-risk and longevity guides. This article explains the schedule of a transition; those additional questions concern uncertain return order and how long a wider plan must last. A useful review records both the dates that create the largest requests and the assumptions that could make those requests harder to fund.
